etymology: Scottish surname Burns, from a dweller by a burn or brook; the given name William from Germanic Wil-helm, “resolute protector.”
biblical_def: William Chalmers Burns (1815–1868) was a Scottish preacher of the Free Church whom the Lord used to kindle remarkable awakenings at Kilsyth and Dundee, and afterward a missionary to China who laboured the last twenty years of his life largely unseen. He took up Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s pulpit in 1839 and saw God pour out conviction of sin and conversions in numbers that humbled every earthly explanation. Rather than make a career of revival, Burns counted himself a servant of the gospel wherever it was least known, and he sailed for China in 1847, mastering the language, donning native dress, and tramping inland where no English voice was heard. He left no great institution behind, only translated tracts, planted believers, and a younger man named Hudson Taylor, whom he mentored and shaped for the China Inland Mission. Burns embodied the truth that the Lord saves by His Spirit and not by the strength of men; he prayed long, preached plainly, and lived poor. His life answers the modern lie that fruitfulness must be visible and measurable. He died at Niuzhuang, far from home, having spent himself for souls he would not see gathered until the resurrection. His memory rebukes the comfortable and stirs the church to obey the Great Commission at any cost.
webster_summary: A Scottish revival preacher and pioneer missionary to China whose Spirit-wrought awakenings and hidden labours mentored Hudson Taylor.
webster_full: WILLIAM BURNS, a Scottish Free Church preacher (1815–1868) and later missionary to China.
Instrument of the Kilsyth and Dundee awakenings while supplying M’Cheyne’s pulpit in 1839.
Sailed for China in 1847 and laboured there until his death, adopting Chinese dress and speech.
Mentor to Hudson Taylor, founder of the China Inland Mission.
Died at Niuzhuang in 1868, having spent his life in obscure and faithful gospel toil.
scriptures: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
corruption_summary: Burns’ insistence that revival is the sovereign work of the Spirit, not a technique, stands against every manufactured substitute.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Burns is that genuine awakening is the gift of God’s Spirit answering prayer and plain preaching, not the product of method, music, or emotional manipulation. He sought no platform and built no machinery; he preached Christ crucified and waited on the Lord.

His willingness to bury his gifts in unseen Chinese labour rebukes a church addicted to visible results. Burns reminds us that the seed sown in tears is reaped at the resurrection, and that the sending of preachers is the Lord’s appointed means for the salvation of the nations.
roots_summary: The name joins Germanic “resolute protector” with a Scots word for a running brook.
roots_lines: William Burns — William from Wil-helm, “resolute protector”; Burns, dweller by a brook.
Bore the middle name Chalmers, after the great Scottish divine Thomas Chalmers.
Title often given him: the “Apostle of Kilsyth.”
His Chinese labours rooted the gospel inland before treaty ports were widely open.
His mentorship is the living root of the China Inland Mission through Hudson Taylor.
usage: When the Spirit fell at Kilsyth, William Burns stood astonished that God should work so mightily through so weak a vessel.
Like William Burns, the true missionary covets souls more than success.
Hudson Taylor learned faith and self-denial at the side of William Burns.

etymology: Gladys from a Welsh name long linked with gladness; Aylward, an Old English surname meaning “noble guardian.”
biblical_def: Gladys Aylward (1902–1970) was an English parlour-maid whom no mission board would accept, yet who spent her own meagre savings on a one-way rail ticket across Siberia to reach China in 1932. Rejected as unqualified, she went anyway, convinced that the Lord who calls also equips. She settled at Yangcheng, opened with an older missionary the Inn of the Eighth Happiness, and there told gospel stories to muleteers passing through the mountains. She learned the language, was appointed a government foot-inspector to end the binding of girls’ feet, and used the office to preach Christ in every village she entered. When the Japanese invasion swept the province, Aylward led roughly a hundred orphaned children on a desperate trek over the mountains and across the Yellow River to safety, half-starved and footsore, singing as they went. Her life is a standing rebuke to the notion that God only uses the credentialed and the strong. She was small, poor, and unschooled, and the Lord made her a deliverer of children and a herald of the cross. Becoming a Chinese citizen, she gave her whole life to a people not her own. Her courage flowed not from temperament but from faith in a sovereign God who keeps His servants until their work is done.
webster_summary: An English maidservant turned missionary to China, called “The Small Woman,” who led a hundred orphans over the mountains to safety.
webster_full: GLADYS AYLWARD, an English missionary to China (1902–1970), known as “The Small Woman.”
Rejected by a mission board, she paid her own way across Siberia to reach China in 1932.
Helped run the Inn of the Eighth Happiness at Yangcheng, preaching to passing travellers.
Served as a government foot-inspector, ending foot-binding and spreading the gospel.
Led about a hundred orphaned children over the mountains to safety during the Japanese invasion.
scriptures: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
Mat 18:5
And whoso shall receive one such little child in my name receiveth me.
Isa 6:8
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
Psa 68:5
A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
corruption_summary: Her story refutes the modern gatekeeping that measures a servant’s fitness by credentials rather than by calling and faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Aylward is that God chooses the weak and unqualified to confound the mighty. The boards turned her away; the Lord sent her, and through one rejected woman delivered orphans and gathered souls. Fitness for service is conferred by Christ, not by the approval of men.

Her care for the fatherless flows straight from the heart of God, the father of the fatherless. In an age that prizes self-fulfilment, Aylward spent herself for children who could repay her nothing, becoming a citizen of a foreign land for the sake of the gospel.
roots_summary: A Welsh name of gladness joined to an Old English surname meaning “noble guardian.”
roots_lines: Gladys Aylward — Gladys, linked with gladness; Aylward, “noble guardian.”
Known in China by the name Ai-weh-deh, “the virtuous one.”
Title that clung to her: “The Small Woman,” for her tiny stature.
Her foot-inspector office became a roving pulpit across the villages.
Her mountain trek with the orphans became her most enduring earthly memorial.
usage: Gladys Aylward proved that a sovereign God needs no permission from a board to call His servant.
Footsore and singing, the children followed Gladys Aylward over the last ridge to safety.
When men called her unqualified, Gladys Aylward answered only to the One who sent her.

etymology: Eric from Old Norse, “ever-ruler” or “sole ruler”; Liddell, an English surname from a dweller in a loud valley or by the river Liddel.
biblical_def: Eric Liddell (1902–1945) was a Scottish sprinter, son of missionaries to China, who refused to run his strongest event at the 1924 Paris Olympics because the heats fell on the Lord’s Day. Rather than profane the Sabbath for a medal, he stepped aside, trained for the 400 metres instead, and won gold in a then-record time, declaring that God honoured those who honoured Him. He had already learned that the Lord deserved obedience above applause. At the height of athletic fame Liddell turned from the track to the mission field, returning in 1925 to China where he had been born, to teach and preach the gospel he loved. He laboured in Tianjin and later among the rural poor, never trading the cross for the comforts his celebrity might have bought. When war came, he sent his wife and children to safety and stayed at his post, and was interned by the Japanese at Weihsien camp. There, even in hunger and disease, he organised, served, taught the young, and gave away his own rations, until he died of a brain tumour in 1945 a few months before liberation. His was a life that ran a far longer race than any stadium could measure, finishing the course in faith.
webster_summary: A Scottish Olympic champion who would not race on the Lord’s Day, then gave his fame to missionary labour in China, dying in a Japanese internment camp.
webster_full: ERIC LIDDELL, a Scottish runner and missionary to China (1902–1945).
Refused to run the 100 metres heats at the 1924 Olympics because they fell on the Sabbath.
Won the 400 metres gold instead, in a record time, honouring the God he served.
Returned to China in 1925 as a missionary teacher and preacher.
Died in 1945 at the Weihsien internment camp, having spent himself in service to fellow prisoners.
scriptures: Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
for them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed.
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: Liddell’s Sabbath stand and his surrender of fame rebuke an age that bows the Lord’s claims to ambition and convenience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Liddell is that obedience to God outranks every prize the world can offer. He would not run on the day the Lord set apart, and the world that mocked his scruple was answered by his victory. The fourth commandment was no relic to him but a delight.

Greater still was his choice to leave the applause of nations for the obscurity of the mission field, and finally to pour out his life for fellow captives. His example dismantles the modern idol of self-realisation; he ran to obtain an incorruptible crown, and finished his course keeping the faith.
roots_summary: A Norse name meaning “ever-ruler” joined to a surname from a loud valley or the river Liddel.
roots_lines: Eric Liddell — Eric, “ever-ruler”; Liddell, dweller in a loud valley.
Born in Tianjin, China, to missionary parents of the London Missionary Society.
Nicknamed “the Flying Scotsman” for his speed.
His running style, head thrown back, became as famous as his Sabbath conviction.
His final labours at Weihsien rooted his memory in self-giving rather than in medals.
usage: Eric Liddell would sooner forfeit a gold medal than dishonour the Lord’s Day.
The crowd cheered the sprinter, but Eric Liddell ran for a crown that cannot fade.
Even starving in the camp, Eric Liddell gave his rations away and taught the children to pray.

etymology: Ann (Nancy) from Hebrew Hannah, “grace, favour”; Judson, an English patronymic surname, “son of Jordan or Jud.”
biblical_def: Ann Hasseltine Judson (1789–1826), called Nancy, was the first wife of Adoniram Judson and among the first American women to give her life to foreign missions. Marrying Adoniram in 1812, she sailed within days for the East, embracing a vocation she knew might cost her everything. Settling at last in Burma, she mastered the language, taught women and children, translated portions of Scripture and Gospel tracts, and bore the long, fruitless first years when not a single Burmese believed. Her endurance was tested beyond most men’s. When war broke out and Adoniram was cast into the fetid death-prison at Ava, Ann walked daily to the prison, bribing guards, carrying food, hiding his precious Bible translation in a pillow, pleading for his life while herself wracked with fever and nursing an infant. Her tireless intercession under filth and threat preserved both her husband and his work. She did not live to see the harvest; she died at Amherst in 1826, worn out at thirty-six, soon followed by their child. Yet her letters home stirred a generation of churches to the cause of missions, and the Burmese church that rose owes its first seeds in part to her labours and tears. She is a pattern of the missionary wife who counts Christ worth her life.
webster_summary: The first wife of Adoniram Judson and a pioneer American missionary to Burma, whose endurance and intercession preserved her imprisoned husband and stirred the churches.
webster_full: ANN JUDSON, pioneer American missionary to Burma (1789–1826), wife of Adoniram Judson.
Sailed for the East in 1812, among the first American women on the foreign field.
Learned Burmese, taught women and children, and helped translate Scripture and tracts.
Sustained her husband through his long imprisonment at Ava during the Anglo-Burmese war.
Died at Amherst in 1826, worn out at thirty-six, having sown seeds of the Burmese church.
scriptures: Rev 2:10
be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
Psa 30:5
weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
corruption_summary: Her self-spending labour rebukes an age that treats the missionary calling as colonial overreach rather than obedient love.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Ann Judson is that the Great Commission is worth a woman’s whole life laid down. She crossed the world, learned a hard tongue, buried her children, and wore herself out, all to bring the gospel to a people who at first wanted none of it. Such love is no imposition but the overflow of grace received.

Where modern voices would recast pioneer missions as cultural conquest, her story tells the truth: she came not to take but to give, not to rule but to serve, carrying the only news that saves. Faithful unto death, she earned the crown of life and left a church behind her.
roots_summary: Hebrew “grace” joined to an English patronymic surname.
roots_lines: Ann Judson — Ann from Hannah, “grace, favour”; Judson, “son of Jud.”
Born Ann Hasseltine in Bradford, Massachusetts; known affectionately as Nancy.
Married Adoniram Judson on 5 February 1812, sailing within two weeks.
Hid her husband’s Burmese Bible manuscript from prison guards.
Her published letters helped ignite the American foreign-missions movement.
usage: Ann Judson carried food to the Ava death-prison day after day while burning with fever.
Few endured the first barren years of Burma as faithfully as Ann Judson.
The letters of Ann Judson awakened American congregations to the unreached.

etymology: Pandita, a Sanskrit honorific for a learned woman, “scholar”; Ramabai, joining the divine name Rama with the respectful bai, “lady.”
biblical_def: Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) was an Indian woman of high learning, born to a Brahmin scholar who broke custom by teaching his daughter the Sanskrit scriptures. Orphaned young and widowed early, she rose to rare renown as a Sanskrit teacher, granted the title Pandita for her mastery. Yet the systems she had studied gave her no answer to the misery of India’s child-widows and abandoned women, and her searching led her to Christ, in whom she found the living God the idols could not give. She was baptised in 1883 and ever after confessed Jesus as Saviour and Lord. Settling near Pune, she founded the Mukti Mission, a refuge that in time sheltered thousands of widows, orphans, and famine victims, where they were fed, taught a trade, and above all told of the Saviour. She translated the whole Bible into Marathi from the original tongues, that her people might read the Scriptures plainly. A revival of prayer and confession swept Mukti in 1905. Ramabai never softened the gospel to suit her culture; she named the bondage of caste and idolatry and held up Christ as the only deliverer. Her life joined rigorous learning, fierce compassion, and a settled faith in the God who hears the cry of the helpless.
webster_summary: An Indian Brahmin scholar converted to Christ who founded the Mukti Mission for widows and orphans and translated the Bible into Marathi.
webster_full: PANDITA RAMABAI, an Indian Christian scholar and reformer (1858–1922).
Born to a Brahmin family and granted the title Pandita for her Sanskrit learning.
Converted to Christ and baptised in 1883 after the idols gave her no hope.
Founded the Mukti Mission near Pune, a refuge for widows, orphans, and the famine-stricken.
Translated the whole Bible into Marathi from the original languages.
scriptures: Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
The LORD preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow:
Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Isa 1:17
Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
corruption_summary: Her unflinching naming of idolatry and caste as bondage rebukes the modern habit of treating false religions as parallel paths to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Ramabai is that pure and undefiled religion cares for the widow and the fatherless and confesses Christ as the only Saviour. She did not blend her old learning with the gospel; she renounced the idols that had failed her and clung to the Son who makes free indeed.

Her Mukti Mission joined mercy to truth, sheltering the helpless body while preaching the saving word. Against every claim that all faiths lead alike to God, her life testifies that she found in Christ what the systems of men could never supply, and spent herself that others might find Him too.
roots_summary: A Sanskrit honorific for a learned woman joined to a respectful Indian name.
roots_lines: Pandita Ramabai — Pandita, “learned woman, scholar”; bai, “lady.”
The title Pandita was conferred for her public mastery of the Sanskrit scriptures.
Mukti, the name of her mission, means “salvation” or “deliverance.”
Her Marathi Bible was rendered directly from the Hebrew and Greek.
A revival of confession and prayer broke out at Mukti in 1905.
usage: Pandita Ramabai turned her rare learning to the service of India’s forsaken widows.
The idols had no answer for Pandita Ramabai, but Christ set her free.
Thousands of orphans found bread and the gospel at the Mukti Mission of Pandita Ramabai.

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps “firstborn” or “shadow from terror,” the precise meaning uncertain.
biblical_def: Zelophehad was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Hepher and descendant of Joseph through Machir and Gilead, who came up out of Egypt and died in the wilderness during the years of Israel’s wandering. Scripture is careful to record that he did not perish in the rebellion of Korah, who gathered himself against the LORD, but died in his own sin, the common lot of that faithless generation barred from Canaan. What sets Zelophehad apart is what he left behind: he had no sons, but five daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. In an order where the inheritance passed through sons, his line stood to be blotted out and his portion in the land lost. His daughters brought the matter before Moses, Eleazar, and the whole congregation, and the LORD Himself ruled that they should receive their father’s inheritance, establishing a lasting statute in Israel. Thus an otherwise obscure man, who did nothing recorded but die, became the occasion of a divine law that secured a family’s place among the tribes. His brief notice teaches that the LORD governs the smallest matters of inheritance and lineage, that no faithful name need be forgotten in His providence, and that even in a generation under judgment God remembers households and keeps their portion in the land He swore to give.
webster_summary: A man of Manasseh who died in the wilderness leaving five daughters and no sons, whose case prompted God’s statute on female inheritance.
webster_full: ZELOPHEHAD, a man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Hepher.
Came out of Egypt and died in the wilderness, not in Korah’s rebellion (Num 27:3).
Left no sons but five daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah (Num 26:33).
His daughters’ plea led the LORD to grant them their father’s inheritance (Num 27:7).
His case fixed a lasting statute of inheritance in Israel.
scriptures: And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters: and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, and Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.
Num 27:3
Our father died in the wilderness, and he was not in the company of them that gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah; but died in his own sin, and had no sons.
Num 27:7

The daughters of Zelophehad speak right: thou shalt surely give them a possession of an inheritance among their father’s brethren; and thou shalt cause the inheritance of their father to pass unto them.
Jos 17:3

But Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, had no sons, but daughters: and these are the names of his daughters, Mahlah, and Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.
corruption_summary: His brief record shows the LORD’s providence over lineage and inheritance, even for a man who did nothing notable but die in faith’s generation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Zelophehad is that the providence of God reaches into the most ordinary lives, securing a family’s portion in the promised land through a man who left only daughters and a name. The smallest matters of inheritance lie under the LORD’s care.

Scripture’s care to note that he died in his own sin and not in Korah’s rebellion is a sober word: every man of that generation died short of Canaan, yet God remembered the household and kept its place. No faithful name is lost in His reckoning.
roots_summary: A Hebrew name of uncertain sense, perhaps “firstborn” or “shadow from terror.”
roots_lines: Zelophehad — Hebrew, perhaps “firstborn” or “shadow from terror.”
Descended through Hepher, Gilead, Machir, to Manasseh son of Joseph.
His name survives chiefly because of his five daughters.
Named in Numbers, Joshua, and the genealogy of 1 Chronicles.
His case is paired with the later statute of Numbers 36 on tribal inheritance.
usage: Zelophehad left no sons, yet his portion in the land was not lost.
The plea of Zelophehad’s daughters drew from the LORD a lasting statute.
Even an obscure man like Zelophehad stands as proof that God orders every lineage.

etymology: Their father’s name is Hebrew, of uncertain sense; their own names — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah — carry meanings such as “weakness,” “motion,” “partridge,” “queen,” and “pleasantness.”
biblical_def: The daughters of Zelophehad — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — were five sisters of the tribe of Manasseh whose father died in the wilderness leaving no sons. As Israel stood on the plains of Moab numbering the tribes for the division of Canaan, they saw their father’s name in danger of being blotted out and his inheritance lost, for the land was to pass through sons. With courage and reverence they came and stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the princes, and all the congregation at the door of the tabernacle, and made their plea: let their father’s portion be given to them. Moses did not presume to answer of himself but brought their cause before the LORD. God ruled that the daughters spoke right, and commanded that they receive their father’s inheritance, establishing through their case a perpetual statute for Israel. Later, when the heads of Gilead feared the land might pass from the tribe by their marriage, the LORD added the just provision that they marry within their own tribe, so that the inheritance should not move from one tribe to another. The sisters obeyed. Their account honours godly order while showing the LORD’s care that no faithful family lose its place; they sought their portion lawfully, through the appointed authorities, and God Himself secured them.
webster_summary: Five sisters of Manasseh — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — whose lawful plea for their father’s inheritance prompted a divine statute.
webster_full: DAUGHTERS OF ZELOPHEHAD, five sisters of the tribe of Manasseh.
Their names were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah (Num 27:1).
They came before Moses and the congregation seeking their father’s inheritance.
The LORD judged that they spoke right and granted their request (Num 27:7).
They later married within their own tribe to keep the inheritance in Manasseh (Num 36:11).
scriptures: Num 27:1

Then came the daughters of Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, of the families of Manasseh the son of Joseph: and these are the names of his daughters; Mahlah, Noah, and Hoglah, and Milcah, and Tirzah.
Num 27:7

The daughters of Zelophehad speak right: thou shalt surely give them a possession of an inheritance among their father’s brethren; and thou shalt cause the inheritance of their father to pass unto them.
Num 36:6
This is the thing which the LORD doth command concerning the daughters of Zelophehad, saying, Let them marry to whom they think best; only to the family of the tribe of their father shall they marry.
Jos 17:4

And they came near before Eleazar the priest, and before Joshua the son of Nun, and before the princes, saying, The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brethren. Therefore according to the commandment of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brethren of their father.
corruption_summary: Their case is sometimes seized to overthrow biblical order, when in truth it honours that order while showing God’s care for every household.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from the daughters of Zelophehad is that the LORD secures the portion of the faithful and answers lawful petition. The sisters did not rebel against the appointed authorities; they came reverently before Moses, the priest, and the congregation, and waited on the LORD’s word.

Their account upholds godly order even as it provides for them: God Himself added that they marry within their tribe so the inheritance should not stray. Far from overturning His arrangement of the tribes, their case displays His justice and His tender keeping of households whose name might otherwise have failed in Israel.
roots_summary: Five Hebrew names of varied meaning, bound together by their father’s lost line.
roots_lines: Daughters of Zelophehad — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah, sisters of Manasseh.
Mahlah is often glossed “weakness”; Tirzah, “pleasantness.”
Milcah carries the sense of “queen”; Hoglah, “partridge.”
Tirzah later became the name of a city and an early capital of the northern kingdom.
Their names recur in Numbers, Joshua, and the Chronicles genealogy.
usage: The daughters of Zelophehad sought their inheritance through the appointed authorities, not against them.
By the case of the daughters of Zelophehad the LORD fixed a statute in Israel.
Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah married within Manasseh as God commanded.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “anklet” or “ankle ornament.”
biblical_def: Achsah was the daughter of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, that faithful spy of Judah who with Joshua brought back a good report and wholly followed the LORD. When Israel took the land, Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to the man who would smite Kirjath-sepher, and Othniel his kinsman took the city and won her as his wife. He afterward became the first of Israel’s judges. Achsah’s brief account is best known for her wisdom and boldness in seeking a fuller blessing. Given a portion in the dry land of the south, she urged Othniel and then came herself to her father, lighting from her donkey before him, and asked a blessing: since he had given her a south land, let him also give her springs of water. Caleb, far from rebuffing her, granted her the upper springs and the nether springs, that her inheritance might bear fruit. Her request was no greedy demand but a daughter’s reverent petition for what would make the gift truly useful. She honoured her father and received from his hand. Achsah stands as a quiet picture of faith that asks of a generous giver, and of a father who delights to give good things to his children. Her short story rewards the reader who, like her, presses on from a lesser portion to a fuller one.
webster_summary: Caleb’s daughter, given in marriage to Othniel, who reverently asked her father for springs of water to enrich her inheritance.
webster_full: ACHSAH, the daughter of Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
Given in marriage to Othniel, who captured Kirjath-sepher to win her (Jos 15:16).
Her husband Othniel became the first of Israel’s judges (Jdg 3:9).
She asked her father for springs to water her south-land inheritance (Jos 15:19).
Caleb granted her the upper and the nether springs.
scriptures: And Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjath-sepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.
And it came to pass, as she came unto him, that she moved him to ask of her father a field: and she lighted off her ass; and Caleb said unto her, What wouldest thou?
Who answered, Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs, and the nether springs.
Jdg 1:15
And she said unto him, Give me a blessing: for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs.
corruption_summary: Her reverent asking and Caleb’s ready giving picture the faith that seeks good gifts from a generous father.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Achsah is the boldness of faith that asks. She did not murmur over a dry portion but came to her father and sought the springs that would make it fruitful, and he granted her abundance. So the children of God are bidden to ask of a Father who gives liberally.

Her story also honours godly order: she came lighting from her donkey, addressing her father with reverence, and received from his hand. There is no rebellion here, only a daughter’s wise petition met by a father’s glad generosity, a small portrait of grace freely sought and freely given.
roots_summary: A Hebrew name meaning “anklet” or ornament for the ankle.
roots_lines: Achsah — Hebrew, “anklet,” an ornament for the ankle.
Daughter of Caleb of the tribe of Judah.
Wife of Othniel, Israel’s first judge and deliverer.
Her account appears in both Joshua and Judges.
The springs she asked were the upper and the nether springs of the south.
usage: Achsah lighted from her donkey and asked her father for a blessing.
Caleb gave Achsah both the upper and the nether springs to water her land.
Like Achsah, the believer presses from a dry portion to ask for living water.

etymology: Tekoa, a town of Judah south of Bethlehem, from a Hebrew root meaning “a pitching of tents” or “a trumpet blast.”
biblical_def: The woman of Tekoa was a wise woman whom Joab fetched from her town when he perceived that King David’s heart was toward his banished son Absalom. After Absalom had slain his brother Amnon and fled, David mourned but would not recall him. Joab, seeking the king’s relief and his own ends, sent for this woman of discernment and put words in her mouth. Feigning to be a widow in mourning, she came before David with a parable: her two sons had quarrelled in the field, the one slew the other, and now the whole family demanded the survivor’s life, which would quench the last coal left to her and cut off her husband’s name. David, moved, swore to protect her son. Then with great skill she turned his own ruling against him, showing that he had passed sentence on himself while keeping his banished one shut out, and pleaded that God devises means that His banished be not expelled from Him. David discerned Joab’s hand in it, yet granted the substance, and Absalom was brought home. The woman’s wisdom is a study in persuasive, reverent speech that pierces a king’s conscience. Her famous words, that God contrives ways to bring back the outcast, breathe a deeper gospel hope than she perhaps knew, of a God who recalls the banished through a Mediator.
webster_summary: A wise woman sent by Joab to King David with a parable, persuading him to recall his banished son Absalom.
webster_full: THE WOMAN OF TEKOA, a wise woman of Judah employed by Joab.
Joab sent for her to move David’s heart toward the banished Absalom (2Sa 14:2).
She came in mourning attire and told the king a parable of her two sons.
She turned David’s own ruling to plead for the king’s exiled son (2Sa 14:13).
Her words led to Absalom’s recall to Jerusalem.
scriptures: And Joab sent to Tekoah, and fetched thence a wise woman, and said unto her, I pray thee, feign thyself to be a mourner, and put on now mourning apparel, and anoint not thyself with oil, but be as a woman that had a long time mourned for the dead:

And the woman said, Wherefore then hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God? for the king doth speak this thing as one which is faulty, in that the king doth not fetch home again his banished.

For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him.
To fetch about this form of speech hath thy servant Joab done this thing: and my lord is wise, according to the wisdom of an angel of God, to know all things that are in the earth.
corruption_summary: Her parable, especially her word that God devises means that His banished be not expelled, carries a gospel hope of the outcast recalled.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from the woman of Tekoa is the power of wise, reverent speech to pierce a conscience, and the gospel glimpse in her words. She spoke of a God who devises means that His banished be not expelled from Him, a truth fulfilled in Christ, through whom the outcast sinner is brought home.

Her account also instructs in discernment: David saw Joab’s hand behind her errand yet weighed the substance of her plea. Persuasion need not be deceit when it serves truth, though here it was bent to Joab’s designs. The enduring word is hers: the God of Israel contrives the recall of the banished.
roots_summary: Named for Tekoa, a Judean town meaning “a pitching of tents” or “a trumpet blast.”
roots_lines: The Woman of Tekoa — Tekoa, “a pitching of tents” or “trumpet blast.”
Tekoa lay in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem.
The same town was later home to the prophet Amos.
She is called a “wise woman,” a recognised office of counsel in Israel.
Her speech compared David’s wisdom to that of an angel of God.
usage: The woman of Tekoa came before David in mourning to plead a feigned cause.
By her parable the woman of Tekoa turned the king’s own judgment toward Absalom.
Few have spoken a deeper gospel word than the woman of Tekoa concerning God’s banished.

etymology: From the Hebrew, connected with the word for sorrow or pain, “he causes pain,” because his mother bore him in sorrow.
biblical_def: Jabez appears in a single brief passage tucked within the genealogies of Judah in First Chronicles, yet his record shines for its honour and its prayer. Scripture says he was more honourable than his brethren, though his mother had named him Jabez, saying she bore him in sorrow. Despite a name that marked him with pain from birth, Jabez did not resign himself to sorrow but called on the God of Israel, praying that God would bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand upon him, and keep him from evil that it might not grieve him. The text simply adds that God granted him that which he requested. His prayer is no charm or formula for prosperity, as some have wrongly made it, but a humble appeal to the sovereign God who hears His people, asking for blessing, for usefulness, for the LORD’s presence, and above all for keeping from evil. It is the cry of faith that depends wholly on God for everything good and dreads sin more than hardship. That such a man should be honoured above his brethren and singled out in the dry rolls of genealogy testifies that the LORD marks the prayers of the lowly. Jabez teaches that no name and no painful beginning can shut a man out from the grace of a God who answers those who call upon Him in faith.
webster_summary: A man of Judah, more honourable than his brethren, whose humble prayer for blessing, enlargement, and keeping from evil God granted.
webster_full: JABEZ, a man of the tribe of Judah named in the Chronicles genealogy.
Called more honourable than his brethren (1Ch 4:9).
Named by his mother for the sorrow in which she bore him.
Prayed that God would bless him, enlarge his coast, and keep him from evil (1Ch 4:10).
God granted him that which he requested.
scriptures: And Jabez was more honourable than his brethren: and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bare him with sorrow.

And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.
The eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry.
Jer 33:3
Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.
corruption_summary: His prayer, abused by some as a prosperity formula, is in truth the humble appeal of faith to a God who answers those who call.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to name here is the misuse of his prayer as a self-help charm for wealth and success. The text shows no formula but a believer casting himself wholly on the God of Israel, asking for blessing, for the LORD’s hand upon him, and above all to be kept from evil lest it grieve him.

Read rightly, Jabez teaches that God hears the cry of the lowly and that no painful beginning can bar a man from grace. His chief petition was holiness, not gain; he dreaded sin more than hardship. The honour Scripture gives him belongs to the faith that prays and the God who answers, not to any technique for prosperity.
roots_summary: A Hebrew name bound to the word for sorrow or pain, given because of a sorrowful birth.
roots_lines: Jabez — Hebrew, linked with sorrow or pain, “he causes pain.”
His mother gave the name because she bore him with sorrow (1Ch 4:9).
A man of the tribe of Judah in the Chronicles genealogy.
A town of scribes in Judah also bore the name Jabez (1Ch 2:55).
His whole record stands in two short verses, yet is among the most quoted of prayers.
usage: Jabez was more honourable than his brethren though his name spoke of sorrow.
The prayer of Jabez asked for blessing and for keeping from evil, not for mere gain.
Like Jabez, the believer calls on the God of Israel and is heard.
